AI is rapidly reshaping recycling workflows and documentation, but people still carry responsibility for on-site judgment and professional experience. This article explains the specific impact and response paths.

It does not suit people who avoid dirt and hard work, cannot tolerate odors and noise, or dislike conveyors. Recycling sites are often wet, smelly, and loud, making the work difficult for sensitive people.
A common path is: begin in frontline operations, learn equipment, become sorting team leader, manage a production line, then advance to site supervisor or quality inspection.

paragraphs: In the morning, put on protective equipment and inspect the line, then sort plastic, paper, and metal at the conveyor. At midday, operate crushing and baling equipment and watch for contaminants and hazardous waste. In the afternoon, clean the site, maintain equipment, and bale by category. Before leaving, record output and anomalies for handoff.

In one sentence: turn waste into resources. Duties include sorting, crushing, removing hazardous waste, maintaining equipment, baling, and recording output. The work combines hands and eyes at the front end of the recycling cycle.

Moderately high exposure does not mean high risk. Manual sorting of standard materials is being replaced, not on-site handling. Workers who operate equipment and manage hazardous waste become scarcer as automation grows. Those who only perform template-based sorting face the greatest risk.
